opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and I think it gets at something really fundamental. LLMs are incredibly good at what I'd call world knowledge or common sense: they've read the internet, so they know roughly how things work in general. But most of the decisions that actually matter in a business aren't common-sense decisions. They're decisions that depend on *your* data. Which customer is likely to churn next month? How much inventory should we stock in this particular store? Which transaction looks fraudulent? Will this patient be readmitted? An LLM has never seen your customers, your transactions, your supply chain. So no amount of reasoning in language is going to give you a calibrated answer there.

So the way I think about it is that agents need access to a different kind of tool: predictive models that are grounded in the organization's own data. And the interesting thing is where that data lives. It lives in relational databases and data warehouses: tables of customers, orders, products, events, all linked together through keys. That's really a graph. Each row is a node, the foreign-key relationships are edges, and there's a temporal dimension as well.

Historically, if you wanted a prediction on that data, you'd have a data science team spend weeks or months doing feature engineering, joining tables, aggregating, training a model for each task. That doesn't work for an agent, which needs to ask a new predictive question on the fly. So the direction we've been pushing is what we call relational foundation models: models pretrained to learn directly over the structure of relational data, using graph neural networks and graph transformers, so that you can pose a predictive question, almost like a query, and get an accurate prediction back without building a bespoke pipeline each time.

Then the picture for agents becomes quite clean. The LLM is the reasoning and orchestration layer. It understands the user's intent, breaks the problem down, decides what it needs to know. But when it needs a quantitative prediction about the future based on the company's data, it calls out to a predictive model as a tool, the same way it might call a calculator or a search engine. You get the best of both: the LLM's flexibility and language understanding, plus models that are actually accurate on structured, private, enterprise data.

And I'd add that this matters a lot for trust. If an agent is going to take actions, like offering a discount, flagging a transaction, or reordering stock, you want those actions driven by a calibrated prediction you can evaluate and backtest, not by the LLM's guess about what sounds plausible. Separating "reasoning about what to do" from "predicting what will happen" is, I think, the key architectural step for making agents useful in real decision-making.

r001.rationale: The response says agents should use predictive models for quantitative predictions about the future and base actions on calibrated predictions, separating prediction of outcomes from reasoning about actions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about this is that the LLM, out of the box, is really a reasoning engine over whatever happens to be in its parameters. It has absorbed a huge amount of common sense from the web, and that's incredibly useful. But the moment an agent has to make a decision that depends on something specific — your company's data, a particular customer's history, what's actually in this hospital's records today — common sense isn't enough. The model simply doesn't know, and when it doesn't know, it tends to confabulate rather than admit that.

So the question becomes: how do you ground the agent in the real data, and how do you let it reason over that data in a way that's actually reliable?

My view is that retrieval alone, in the sense of pulling in a few text chunks, is a pretty shallow answer. Most of the data that matters for real decisions isn't a pile of documents. It's structured. It's relational. It lives in databases with tables and foreign keys, it's events over time, it's entities and relationships between them — it's really a graph. A customer is connected to orders, which are connected to products, which are connected to suppliers, and so on. And the decision you want to make — will this customer churn, is this transaction fraudulent, which patient is at risk — depends on patterns across all of those connections, not on any single record.

So I think agents need two things beyond the LLM. One is a way to actually reach into those systems and ask precise questions — call a tool, run a query, get back a fact rather than a guess. And the second, which I think is underappreciated, is that some decisions aren't lookups at all. They're predictions. No amount of querying tells you what will happen next quarter. For that you need a model that has actually learned from the structure of the data — and this is where things like graph neural networks and what we've been calling relational foundation models come in. You can pretrain a model directly on relational data, across many databases, and then it can make these predictions on a new database without task-specific training, in the same way an LLM generalizes across text.

So the picture I have is a kind of division of labor. The LLM handles the language, the planning, the orchestration — understanding what the user wants and decomposing it. But when it hits a question that requires a specific fact, it queries. And when it hits a question that requires a forecast or a judgment grounded in historical patterns, it should call out to a model that's been trained on that kind of data and get back a calibrated answer, ideally with some notion of confidence. The agent then reasons over those outputs, rather than trying to hallucinate the answer from priors.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that the agent needs to know which regime it's in. A lot of the failures we see are the model answering a prediction question as if it were a common-sense question. Teaching agents to recognize "this is something I should look up," versus "this is something I should predict with a specialized model," versus "this is something I can reason about directly" — I think that's actually a big part of what makes an agent trustworthy.

r001.rationale: The response advocates using specialized models to forecast outcomes such as churn, fraud, or patient risk. It does not clearly say agents should estimate the downstream effects of the decisions they make.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between understanding a task and knowing which action to take. An LLM can help interpret what you’re asking, break the problem into steps, and identify tools. But if the decision depends on a particular environment, common sense alone isn’t enough. You need data about that environment, some way to predict the consequences of different actions, and an objective against which to compare them.

For example, if an agent is deciding how to allocate resources, it needs to understand the constraints and tradeoffs. It could use a predictive model to estimate outcomes and an optimization algorithm to choose an action. The LLM can coordinate those components, but it shouldn’t have to invent the answer from its language knowledge.

And then you need a feedback loop: take an action, observe what happens, and update. So I would think of the agent as a system that combines language, prediction, planning, and learning from experience.

r001.rationale: The response says agents need a way to predict the consequences of different actions, directly communicating the need to estimate downstream effects.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between knowing something about the world and understanding what will happen if you take a particular action. An LLM can give you a plausible answer based on common sense, but that may not be enough to make a good decision in a specific environment.

So an agent needs a way to ground its decisions in that environment. What is the current state? What actions are available? What are the consequences, and how uncertain are we about them? That might involve querying data, calling a specialized model, or running a simulation. Then the agent can compare alternatives against an explicit objective, rather than simply choosing the action that sounds most reasonable.

And it needs feedback. You take an action, observe what actually happened, and update your understanding. To me, that loop—reasoning, acting, observing, and learning—is what makes this a decision-making system.

r001.rationale: The response says agents should assess what will happen after an action, including its consequences and uncertainty, and may use simulations to do so.
